title: AI for Beginners
subtitle: How a machine learns from its teacher: the true story of Queen
author: Marko Bosko (Mantra Productions)
eyebrow: A free illustrated book · Mantra Productions
byline: Written by Queen (Qwen), corrected by Claude (Opus), commissioned by Marko Bosko
byline_html:
Written by Queen (Qwen) · corrected by Claude (Opus)
Commissioned by Marko Boško · free for everyone
description: A free illustrated book for complete beginners: what an AI language model is, how a student AI (Qwen) learns from a teacher AI (Claude), and what fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA mean, told through one true story with real numbers.
cover_alt: A pencil sketch on cream paper: a desk lamp lighting two chairs at one table, a small notebook open between them.
cover_scene: A wooden table seen at eye level, one desk lamp casting a warm circle of light; two chairs facing each other across it, one small and new, one old and worn; an open notebook and a pencil in the middle of the table between them. Quiet, late evening.
sketch_style: A hand-drawn pencil sketch on warm cream paper. Soft graphite lines, light cross-hatching for the shadows, a few loose construction lines left visible, a little smudging, generous empty paper around the subject. Clear and calm, like a page from a good teacher's sketchbook. Black and grey graphite only on the cream paper, no colour. Absolutely no text, no letters, no words, no numbers, no symbols, no logos, no interface elements anywhere in the picture. Landscape format, 3 by 2.

chapters.title: A Visitor from Another Planet
chapters.dek: What a talking machine is, explained from zero
chapters.brief: Welcome the reader from another planet. Explain what a language model is: a program that read a huge part of everything people wrote and learned one trick, guessing the next word very well; done billions of times it looks like thinking. Give two everyday examples of what it can do. Say clearly what it is NOT (not alive, not a person, it can be wrong). Introduce the story: Marko's house, a student AI called Queen and a teacher AI called Claude.
chapters.scene: A traveller in a long coat stands at the open door of an endless library at night; the shelves curve away into the dark; loose pages drift through the air like birds toward the traveller's outstretched hand.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a traveller at the door of an endless library, pages drifting toward an outstretched hand.
chapters.caption: Everything people ever wrote, read by one machine that learned to guess the next word.

chapters.title: The Student and the Teacher
chapters.dek: Queen does the work, Claude checks every step
chapters.brief: Introduce Queen (Qwen on Groq: fast, cheap) and Claude (Opus: slower, careful). Explain Marko's rule of 13 November 2026 (quote him from the facts): the teacher does not do the work, he gives tasks, writes skills, reviews and corrects. Explain why that is clever: the cheap student does the work, the expensive teacher only checks. Explain what a 'yes' and a 'no with a reason' are, and that every one is written down as a lesson.
chapters.scene: A young apprentice sits at a workbench drawing; behind her an old master leans in and points with a pencil at one spot on her drawing; a lamp lights both hands.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: an old master points with a pencil at one spot in a young apprentice's drawing.
chapters.caption: The student does the work. The teacher only points at what must change.

chapters.title: Eleven Rounds of No
chapters.dek: Queen's first big job, and every mistake on the way
chapters.brief: Tell the true story of Queen's first big job (renaming two apps to Mantra Remote Viewing) with the real mistakes from the facts, as a story with tension: placeholders, three steps at once, the short name, the capitals, the broken link, RDP instead of VNC, the invented tool calls. For each, say the rule it left behind. Then tell honestly that the teacher made mistakes too (the deleted line, the bandwidth saver that would freeze a talking face) and how they were caught. End with the result and the lesson: mistakes become rules.
chapters.scene: A desk at night covered with crumpled paper balls; in the middle one smooth, flat sheet lies under the lamp, a pencil resting across it.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: crumpled paper balls around one smooth sheet under a lamp.
chapters.caption: Every crumpled page left a rule behind. The smooth one is what the rules made possible.

chapters.title: Rules She Reads Before Every Answer
chapters.brief: Explain what a 'skill' is in this story: a short written rule the student reads before every answer (for example: never write a placeholder; capitals stay capitals; use only words you are sure of). Explain why this works at once and costs nothing, unlike training. Compare it to a note on the fridge versus going back to school. Say when a rule is enough and when real training is needed (habits a rule cannot fix).
chapters.scene: A kitchen fridge door covered with small handwritten paper notes held by magnets; a hand pins one more note to it.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a hand pinning one more handwritten note to a fridge door full of notes.
chapters.caption: A rule on the fridge works tomorrow morning. School takes longer.

chapters.title: The Library Called Hugging Face
chapters.dek: Where models and lesson books live
chapters.brief: Explain Hugging Face as a giant public library for AI: models (the students), datasets (the lesson books), tools for teaching, and private shelves only you can open. Compare to GitHub for code. Explain what 'open model' means (Qwen can be downloaded and changed by anyone) versus a closed one. Keep it simple, no installation steps.
chapters.scene: Endless tall bookshelves with a rolling ladder; at the end of an aisle a small cabinet with a lock and a key hanging beside it; a single reader at a reading table.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: endless shelves with a ladder, and a small locked cabinet with its key.
chapters.caption: A public library for machines, with one private cabinet that only you can open.

chapters.title: Private Lessons
chapters.brief: Explain fine-tuning: a student who already finished school gets private lessons for one job. Explain SFT, supervised fine-tuning: every lesson comes with the right answer. Use the red mug example from the sources (instruction, Queen's answer, correct answer, feedback). Explain the nudge: shown the right answer thousands of times, the model is adjusted a tiny bit each time. Say clearly that the teacher does not pour his brain into the student; he writes good examples.
chapters.scene: Two exercise books open side by side on a desk: on the left page a hasty scribbled sketch of a mug, on the right page the same mug drawn carefully with its handle and shading; a teacher's pencil between the two pages.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: two open exercise books, a hasty mug and a careful mug, a pencil between them.
chapters.caption: The lesson is the pair: what she wrote, and what it should have been.

chapters.title: The Clip-On Lens
chapters.dek: LoRA: teaching without rebuilding the brain
chapters.brief: Explain that Queen's brain is about 27 billion numbers and changing all of them is like rebuilding a whole camera. Explain LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) as a small clip-on lens: the big brain is frozen, only the small lens learns. Explain why that is good: small files, many lenses for many jobs, swap in a second, the original stays safe.
chapters.scene: An old camera on a table; a hand clips a small extra lens onto its front; a few other small lenses lie beside it in a row.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a hand clipping a small lens onto an old camera, other small lenses beside it.
chapters.caption: The camera stays. Only the little lens learns, and you can keep a drawer full of them.

chapters.title: The Vacuum-Packed Suitcase
chapters.dek: QLoRA: making the big brain fit
chapters.brief: Explain that even a frozen brain must fit in the computer's memory while it learns. Explain QLoRA as squeezing (quantizing) the big brain into a smaller number format first, like vacuum-packing clothes so the suitcase closes, then training the small lens. Use the facts: a small Qwen can be taught on a free 16 GB graphics card (Google Colab); a Mac cannot do this 4-bit training, it needs an NVIDIA card. Say what is lost (a little precision) and what is won (it fits).
chapters.scene: An open suitcase on a bed; neatly rolled clothes pressed flat inside; two hands pressing the lid down so it closes.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: two hands pressing the lid of a suitcase closed over flat-packed clothes.
chapters.caption: Squeeze first, then it fits. A little less room for each thing, and the whole trip goes.

chapters.title: The Exam You Never Saw
chapters.dek: How we know she learned and did not just memorise
chapters.brief: Explain overfitting with a school example: a student who memorised the answers of the practice sheet passes only those questions. Explain the test set: one lesson in ten is locked away and never practised. Explain the blind exam: old Queen and new Queen answer the locked questions, a judge who does not know which is which picks the better answer, and the new version is kept only if it wins at least 60 out of 100.
chapters.scene: An empty exam desk by a window; a sealed envelope with a wax seal in the centre of the desk; one pencil laid neatly beside it.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a sealed envelope and one pencil on an empty exam desk.
chapters.caption: The questions she never practised are the only ones that tell the truth.

chapters.title: The Whole Loop in One House
chapters.dek: From a question to a better student, step by step
chapters.brief: Walk through the whole loop as it really runs in Marko's house, with the true facts: Marko asks; Queen answers and plans; Claude checks every step; every answer, yes, no and correction is saved with a turn number into a private GitHub repository; dataset version 1 was made on 13 November 2026 with 39 lessons; a new version builds itself after every 25 new examples; about 100 good examples are needed to start training; the lens is trained on a graphics card, examined, and kept on a private Hugging Face shelf with a version number. Make it easy to follow, like a recipe.
chapters.scene: A wooden water wheel turning beside a small house; a stream of water runs from a little channel onto the wheel and back into the stream, a full circle; a lantern hangs at the door.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a water wheel beside a small house, the water running in a full circle.
chapters.caption: Questions go in, lessons come out, and the lessons turn the wheel again.

chapters.title: What It Costs
chapters.dek: Renting a mind by the word, or owning a machine
chapters.brief: Explain tokens simply (pieces of words a model reads and writes, and what you pay for). Use the true numbers from the facts: 67 calls cost 0.30 dollars, about 15 dollars a month; renting your own graphics card all month about 245 dollars; paying per second while it works about 40 to 60 dollars; your own server pays off only at about 17 times Marko's use. Draw the conclusion for a beginner: start by renting by the word; own a machine only when you use it a lot or need your own trained lens.
chapters.scene: An old balance scale on a table: on one pan a single small coin, on the other pan a heavy box-shaped machine with cooling fins; the beam tilts toward the machine.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a balance scale with one small coin on one side and a heavy machine on the other.
chapters.caption: A coin a day, or a machine that must be fed all month.

chapters.title: Start Small
chapters.brief: Give the reader a gentle practical path, from the sources: start with a small student model; collect 50 to 200 good corrected examples; write rules (skills) first; keep a locked exam; train a small lens; test it; only then go bigger. Encourage the reader: the knowledge in this book is free and meant to be shared. End with the one-sentence summary from the sources in your own words.
chapters.scene: A small seedling with two leaves growing from a crack between the pages of an open notebook lying on the ground; morning light from the side.
chapters.alt: Pencil sketch: a seedling growing from between the pages of an open notebook.
chapters.caption: Every big student was once a small one with a notebook.

colophon_html:
Written by Queen (Qwen 27B on Groq), chapter by chapter, each one reviewed and corrected by Claude (Opus) before it was kept.
Pencil sketches on cream paper drawn by Gemini on three of Marko's free accounts. No paid image tool was used.

The story is true: the mistakes, the corrections and the numbers are from 12 and 13 November 2026 in Marko's house. Prices change; check them before you spend.

Free to read, free to share. Mantra Productions · Auroville & Croatia · 13 November 2026.
